paper_metadata.title: Quantum-inspired anomaly detection, a QUBO formulation

experiments.description: Quantum-inspired QUBO anomaly detection benchmark on random Gaussian-distributed data with three different standard deviations, evaluated against classical anomaly detectors using ROC AUC.

algorithm.variant: Quantum-inspired anomaly detection via QUBO with linear centroid-distance terms and quadratic neighbor-distance terms

hyperparameters.alpha: weighting parameter for linear vs quadratic terms, learned during training
hyperparameters.A: penalty weight for enforcing sum(x_i)=k, with A > max(Q)
hyperparameters.neighbor_truncation: only k-furthest neighbors used for quadratic terms

problem_formulation.encoding_details: One binary variable x_i per data point; x_i=1 indicates selected outlier. Objective combines distances to centroid and pairwise distances between selected points.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Maximize Q(x, α) = α * sum_i d_i x_i + (1 - α) * sum_{i != j} d_{i,j} x_i x_j, subject to sum_i x_i = k, with penalty term -A(sum_i x_i - k)^2.

problem_instance.description: Three synthetic Gaussian-distributed datasets with different standard deviations.

dataset_specification.description: Random Gaussian distributed data points; three standard deviations tested.

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Each benchmark instance solved using qbsolv; performance measured by ROC AUC.

speedup_claims.caveats: No explicit speedup or complexity advantage is quantified. The paper only states that the method can be solved with simulated quantum annealing, simulated annealing, or any QUBO solver, and discusses potential scalability limitations on near-term QPUs.

experiments.description: Quantum-inspired QUBO anomaly detection benchmark on three MNIST binary anomaly-detection configurations, evaluated against classical anomaly detectors using ROC AUC.

algorithm.variant: Quantum-inspired anomaly detection via QUBO with linear centroid-distance terms and quadratic neighbor-distance terms

hyperparameters.alpha: weighting parameter for linear vs quadratic terms, learned during training
hyperparameters.A: penalty weight for enforcing sum(x_i)=k, with A > max(Q)
hyperparameters.neighbor_truncation: only k-furthest neighbors used for quadratic terms

problem_formulation.encoding_details: One binary variable x_i per data point; x_i=1 indicates selected outlier. Objective combines distances to centroid and pairwise distances between selected points.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Maximize Q(x, α) = α * sum_i d_i x_i + (1 - α) * sum_{i != j} d_{i,j} x_i x_j, subject to sum_i x_i = k, with penalty term -A(sum_i x_i - k)^2.

problem_instance.description: Three MNIST subsets for anomaly detection: 45 samples of digit 0 and 5 samples of digit 9; 45 samples of digit 7 and 5 samples of digit 1; 45 samples of digit 2 and 5 samples of digit 3.

dataset_specification.description: Handwritten digit subsets from MNIST; minority digit treated as outlier in each configuration.

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Each benchmark instance solved using qbsolv; performance measured by ROC AUC.

speedup_claims.caveats: No explicit speedup claim is reported for the MNIST benchmarks. The paper states only that the method was benchmarked against classical anomaly detectors using qbsolv and ROC AUC.

hyperparameters.neighbor_truncation: only k-furthest neighbors used for quadratic terms

problem_instance.description: Credit card fraud detection dataset with highly imbalanced classes; frauds are the anomalies.

dataset_specification.description: European cardholder transactions over two days in September 2013; 492 frauds out of 284,807 transactions (0.172% fraud rate).
